In the podcast, Matthew is voiced by [Andy Serkis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Serkis "Andy Serkis").

In the Netflix series, Matthew is voiced by [Patton Oswalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patton_Oswalt "Patton Oswalt").

**Mervyn "Merv" Pumpkinhead** is Dream's cantankerous, cigar-smoking [janitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janitor "Janitor"): an animated [scarecrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarecrow "Scarecrow") whose head is a [jack-o'-lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack-o%27-lantern "Jack-o'-lantern"). He resembles [Jack Pumpkinhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Pumpkinhead "Jack Pumpkinhead") of [L. Frank Baum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Frank_Baum "L. Frank Baum")'s [Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Oz "Land of Oz") books.

Mervyn is first seen in _[Preludes and Nocturnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Preludes_and_Nocturnes "The Sandman: Preludes and Nocturnes")_, driving a bus on which Dream travels. Thereafter, Merv is in charge of the construction, maintenance, and demolition work in the Dreaming, though he sometimes complains that his job is superfluous because Dream can change any of the Dreaming at will. One issue of the _Dreaming_ spin-off comic focuses on a dreamer who enjoys working under Merv's supervision. Later issues have him assisted by [Abudah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Abudah).

Mervyn was one of the few who took arms against the Furies in _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_, but was easily killed. He is returned to life by the [new Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Hall_/(comics/) "Daniel Hall (comics)") in _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_ who rebuilds his body and grows a new pumpkin to serve as his head.

In a past incarnation shown in _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_, Mervyn was seen to have had a [turnip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnip "Turnip") for a head instead of a pumpkin as pumpkins were not then known in Europe.

[Kevin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Smith "Kevin Smith") voices Mervyn in the podcast adaptation.

In the Netflix series, Mervyn is performed by Nicholas Anscombe and voiced by [Mark Hamill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Hamill "Mark Hamill").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-9)

**Martin Tenbones** is a large [dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog "Dog")\-like dream who is Barbie's companion.

In the podcast, Martin Tenbones is voiced by [Ray Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Porter "Ray Porter").

In the Netflix series, Martin Tenbones is voiced by [Lenny Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_Henry "Lenny Henry").

**Dora** is a dream that has the form of a young girl in her 20s. She can also assume a monstrous form.

**Brute and Glob** are two trouble-making nightmares who try to gain power during Dream's absence. They originally appeared in [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby")'s 1974 _[Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandman_/(DC_Comics/) "Sandman (DC Comics)")_ series, as sidekicks to the title character, and continued as such when [Hector Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Hall "Hector Hall") became the Sandman in _[Infinity Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity_Inc. "Infinity Inc.")_ In the original comics, Brute was similar to [Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thing_/(Marvel_Comics/) "Thing (Marvel Comics)") where he shouted "It's clobberin' time!" and often referred to his Uncle Harry.

In _[The Doll's House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Doll%27s_House "The Sandman: The Doll's House")_, it is revealed that they controlled the Sandmen in secret whereupon Dream exiled them to "the darkness" (a place of imprisonment and, presumably, torture, within the Dreaming).

Near the end of _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_, the Furies tell Dream that they have released his prisoners from the darkness, but Brute and Glob are neither mentioned nor seen in this volume or in _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_.

They next appear in _The Dreaming_ #57–60, _The Sandman Presents: Everything You Always Wanted To Know About Dreams ... But Were Afraid to Ask_, and _[Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)")_ #15, where they attempt to kidnap [Elaine Belloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Belloc "Elaine Belloc").

They subsequently reappear in _[JSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_Society_of_America "Justice Society of America")_ #64, again trying to manipulate a human connected to the Dreaming ([Sandy Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Hawkins "Sandy Hawkins")) into their own "Sandman"; but Daniel Hall returns them to the darkness. The two entities claim this area of darkness is filled with pleasing childhood dreams, which they despise. First appearance: _The Sandman_ vol. 1 #1.

In the podcast, Brute and Glob are voiced by [Kerry Shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Shale "Kerry Shale") and Harry Myers.

In the Netflix series, their role as the manipulator of Jed Walker is replaced by Gault.

**Abudah** is a hulking monstrous dream who often works as Mervyn Pumpkinhead's assistant. Though he was killed by the Three in _The Kindly Ones_, the new Dream revives him.

In _The Dreaming_, Abudah continues to help Mervyn as a member of his crew.

**The Cuckoo** is a parasitic dream who has conquered Barbie's dreamworld in _A Game of You_. She assumes the form of a childhood version of Barbie and uses her self proclaimed "adorableness" to escape from Barbie's dream world, at which point she transforms into a bird.

In the podcast, the Cuckoo is voiced by Sarah Pitard.

**The Fashion Thing** is a minor character whose form changes based on popular fads. She is based on [The Mad Mod Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mad_Mod_Witch "The Mad Mod Witch"), created by Dave Wood and [Jack Sparling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Sparling "Jack Sparling") as the host of _[The Unexpected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unexpected_/(1968_comic_book/) "The Unexpected (1968 comic book)")_, another DC horror title. At the time of her first appearance in _Sandman_, she is a "Mad [Yuppie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuppie "Yuppie") Witch". First appearance: _The Unexpected_ #108. Most of her appearances are relegated to a few panels. She is shown flying on her broom as a Yuppie briefly in issue #2, shown riding her broom in a top hat and tails with bare legs and feet in issue #22, and shown [topless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toplessness "Toplessness") serving a meal to Delirium and Dream in issue #42. She also appears in _The Kindly Ones_.

**Judge Gallows** appears in several issues of _The Dreaming_ including the Special, "Trial and Error". Introduced in _[The Unexpected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unexpected_/(1968_comic_book/) "The Unexpected (1968 comic book)")_ #113 (June–July 1969), he is one of the few DC "mystery" hosts not used by Gaiman.

**The Smiling Man** is a rogue dream entity that is central to the mystery of the "Sandman Nightmare Country" storyline. It has the appearance of a large obese creature with a serpentine tongue, wide grin and mouths in place of eyes. It silently stalks several characters over the course of the story; passively watching their daily lives and is indirectly responsible for several deaths of those who have seen it (victims being assassinated by a pair of assassins under the employ of Desire).

#### Tempto the Intuitor

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Tempto the Intuitor")\]

**Tempto the Intuitor** is a limbless human with hypnosis.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#1-10) His true form is the [Biblical serpent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpents_in_the_Bible "Serpents in the Bible") that tempted Eve who can also assume a humanoid serpent form.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#2._DC_Comics-11) Tempto took Goldie to the Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge in order to get his second chance at Paradise. When Goldie touched it, it brought it and Eve to the [Garden of Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_Eden "Garden of Eden") where Adam also appeared. Unfortunately, Goldie overloaded both trees and freed Eve by the time Cain, Abel, and Gregory caught up to it. Reverted to his limbless human form, Tempto got away.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-12)

**Gus** is a [Minotaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minotaur "Minotaur") who serves as the bartender of the Labyrinth Grill in "The Dreaming Without".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#1-10)

**Anika** is a [Gorgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgons "Gorgons") waitress at the Labyrinth Grill in "The Dreaming Without". She is often annoyed when Tempto the Inuitor stiffs his bill payment.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#1-10)

**Unipod Ed** is a [Unipod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopod_/(creature/) "Monopod (creature)") hunter.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#2._DC_Comics-11)

**Buffo Crapaud** is a humanoid [toad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toad "Toad") and magician who entertains at Doctor Crapaud's Emporium of Ephemera and Magical Accoutrements. He and Matthew walk a woman named Bridget Leary through what happens when one enters someone else's dreams like she did with Chris.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-13)

#### Cartographer of Dreams

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Cartographer of Dreams")\]

The **Cartographer of Dreams** is a human-like character that maps out the different dreams from his observatory in the Shifting Zones.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#36-14)

**Petit Furret** is a [ferret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferret "Ferret")\-like creature that is the pet of the Cartographer of Dreams.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-The_Dreaming_#36-14)

**Daniel Nod** is the assistant librarian to Lucien. Goldie accompanied Daniel Nod on official library business, where they collected the different checked-out fables and folklores books from the residents of the Book Lands. The residents include a bridge troll, a Snidely Whiplash-like villain, [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur "King Arthur"), some Iranian ladies, the [Three Little Pigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Little_Pigs "The Three Little Pigs"), a dying [Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood "Robin Hood"), and [Captain Hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Hook "Captain Hook").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-15)

**Balco** is a [chimpanzee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee "Chimpanzee") mechanic in the Dreaming who tends to the cars that anyone dreams about at the Royal Motor Pool. He provides Mervyn Pumpkinhead with a car to help him in his mission to rescue Dream's stolen sand for Potiphar Flush.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-16)

**Magpie** is a female human who returned to the Dreaming sometime after the original Dream's death. She had lost her left hand somewhere and was searching for her prince.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-17)

**Dora** is a Night Hag and resident of the Dreaming with wings on her ears who is incapable of dreaming.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-18)

**Ziggy** is a member of the Blanks that works for Dora.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-19)

**Taramis** is a human-like character who serves as a butler to Dream. He informs Lucien about the ambassadors from the other realms. He was killed by the Dreaming A.I.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-20)

An unrelated Taramis appears in _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(TV_series/) "The Sandman (TV series)")_ portrayed by [Phoebe Nicholls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_Nicholls "Phoebe Nicholls"). She is the [chef de cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chef_de_cuisine "Chef de cuisine") of the Dreaming who is exclusive to the Netflix series. She was responsible for cooking the food for the event where the demons, gods, fairies, representatives of the Lords of Chaos, and representatives for the Lords of Order were attending to determine who would own the Key to Hell. Taramis was later seen with Lucienne when Nada left the Dreaming.

**Gault** is a shapeshifting nightmare exclusive to the Netflix series who fled the Dreaming in the wake of Morpheus's imprisonment and hides away in the mind of Jed Walker. She created a fantasy world for the boy where he is a superhero known as the "Sandman" as an escape from his uncle Barnaby's abuse in the waking world while posing as his mother Miranda Walker. Gault is eventually tracked down. When confronted reveals her desire to be a dream, Gault wishes to inspire rather than frighten. Before being sent into the Darkness by Dream, Gault states that even nightmares can dream. After Unity Kinkaid's sacrifice, Dream restored Gault as a dream where she now sports butterfly-like wings.

She is analogous to Brute and Glob in the show's version of the story.

Gault is voiced and motion-captured by [Ann Ogbomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Ogbomo "Ann Ogbomo") in her true form and portrayed by [Andi Osho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andi_Osho "Andi Osho") when posing as Miranda Walker in Jed's dreams.

Gods, demigods, and major personifications
------------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=45 "Edit section: Gods, demigods, and major personifications")\]

The following characters are either [gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deity "Deity"), [demigods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demigod "Demigod"), or major personifications:

**Bast**, in [Neil Gaiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gaiman "Neil Gaiman")'s comic book series _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(DC_Comics/Vertigo/) "The Sandman (DC Comics/Vertigo)")_, is the [DC Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Universe "DC Universe") version of the goddess [Bast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bast_/(mythology/) "Bast (mythology)") of [Egyptian mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_mythology "Egyptian mythology"). She was once a major goddess, but the loss of her believers over time has significantly reduced her powers. She is often coquettish toward Dream, who sometimes goes to her for advice or companionship; but she has often claimed never to have been his lover. Bast has also appeared in issues of _[Wonder Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder_Woman "Wonder Woman")_ and _[Hawkgirl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkgirl "Hawkgirl")_, wherein she is one of the chief goddesses worshiped by the Amazons of [Bana-Mighdall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bana-Mighdall "Bana-Mighdall").

Bast appears in _Sandman Presents: Bast: Eternity Game_ (2003), where she attempts to regain her lost power.

In the podcast, Bast is voiced by [Bebe Neuwirth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebe_Neuwirth "Bebe Neuwirth").

### The Presence/The Creator

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=47 "Edit section: The Presence/The Creator")\]

The **Presence** is the _Sandman_ universe's equivalent of a [Supreme Being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God") and he shares many characteristics with the standard Abrahamic God, such as almost never taking a physical form, being a [Creator deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creator_deity "Creator deity"), and having unmatched power. Nevertheless, Gaiman has on several occasions stated that he never intended the Creator to be any specific religion's god, just as he makes it clear in the first appearance of the abode of the angels, the Silver City, that it "is not [Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise "Paradise"). It is not [Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven "Heaven"). It is the Silver City, that is not part of the order of created things", although the Silver City is often identified as "Heaven" in the _Lucifer_ comic book series.

In that series, one of the critical turning points is the Presence's abandonment of his Creation, which leads to a large number of problems, including struggles to claim the power that the Creator has abandoned, to make the destruction of the universe inevitable and to the slow unraveling of the universe due to the disappearance of the Name of the Creator written on every atom in existence. This is an ongoing storyline in _Lucifer_.

**Loki** is a [trickster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trickster "Trickster") god seen in _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Season_of_Mists "The Sandman: Season of Mists")_; based on the [Norse god](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology") [Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki "Loki"). In his own form, Loki is a tall, thin man with yellow eyes and long red hair that resembles flames; but he is capable of assuming any appearance at will. He is sometimes nicknamed 'Lie-Smith' and 'Sky-walker' by other characters.

He is temporarily freed from his punishment by [Odin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odin "Odin") to accompany his negotiations for the rulership of Hell; whereafter he deceives Odin and Thor into imprisoning another god in his place, but fails to fool Dream, who frees the other god and sends a simulacrum of Loki to take his punishment, in exchange for Loki's debt to himself.

Loki returns in _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_, wherein he works with Puck to kidnap Daniel, a child under Dream's protection. The second Corinthian and Matthew eventually find Daniel. Loki attempts to fool them by taking the form of Dream, but the Corinthian strangles Loki and consumes his eyes. A blinded Loki is taken by Odin and Thor back to his punishment.

Loki reappears in _Lucifer_ wherein Lucifer comes to Loki to take his ship for his own universe and destroys the snake that tortures Loki, who therefore allows him the ship.

In the podcast, Loki is voiced by [David Tennant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tennant "David Tennant").

In the Netflix series, Loki is portrayed by [Freddie Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Fox_/(actor/) "Freddie Fox (actor)").

**Odin**, as based on the [Norse God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology") [Odin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odin "Odin"), appears as an old man wearing a wide-brimmed hat, a cloak, and carrying a staff. He is usually depicted as a dark, mysterious figure, missing one eye and accompanied by two ravens named [Huginn and Muninn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huginn_and_Muninn "Huginn and Muninn") ("thought" and "memory"), and two wolves named [Geri and Freki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_and_Freki "Geri and Freki").

Odin appeared in _Season of Mist_ where he, Thor, and Loki partake in the negotiations for the ruler of Hell.

In _The Kindly Ones_, Odin and Thor take Loki back to his punishment for kidnapping Daniel Hall and causing the Three to kill Dream.

In the podcast, Odin is voiced by [Bill Nighy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nighy "Bill Nighy").

In the Netflix series, Odin is portrayed by [Clive Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Russell "Clive Russell"). Unlike the comics, Odin responded to the botched mead-themed summon that the second Corinthian prevented Johanna Constantine from doing and intervened before the Corinthian can eat his eyes.

The **Three** appear in the form of any group of three women; usually the **Mother**, the **[Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden "Maiden")** and the **[Crone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crone "Crone")**, the three aspects of the [Triple Goddess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_deity "Triple deity") in many mythologies. Sometimes, they appear in the form of the three witches from DC's horror anthology _[The Witching Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witching_Hour_/(DC_Comics/) "The Witching Hour (DC Comics)")_: Mildred, Mordred, and Cynthia. As these witches, they also appeared in a [prestige format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_format "Prestige format") limited series of the same title, and two standard limited series, _Witchcraft_ and _Witchcraft: Le Terreur_.

The Three repeatedly appear throughout _The Sandman_, fulfilling different functions at different points in the story. Their first appearance is in _The Sandman_ #2, where they appear as the three witches, Mildred (mother), Mordred (crone), and Cynthia (maiden) from the [DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics") horror anthology _[The Witching Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witching_Hour_/(DC_Comics/) "The Witching Hour (DC Comics)")_. They later take many different forms over the course of the series, and the "three women" symbol remains an extremely common one, often blurring the lines between when characters are supposed to be merely themselves and when they are supposed to be representations of the Three. The Three represent the female principle, prophecy, and mystery, and they are often a vaguely menacing and enigmatic presence in the series. Incarnations of the Three include the [Erinyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erinyes "Erinyes") (Furies) in their vengeful aspect and the [Moirai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moirai "Moirai") (Fates) or [Weird Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_Sisters "Weird Sisters") in their divinatory aspect. They also sometimes subtly appear in the form of other characters (such as [Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eve_/(DC_Comics/) "Eve (DC Comics)")) or groups of characters. Their Erinyes form were responsible for massacring Dream, Abel, Mervyn Pumpkinhead, Abudah Fiddler's Green, and the Griffin Gate Keeper.

The Three later appeared in a graphic novel named _WitchCraft_, in which one of their priestesses in ancient Rome, Ursula, is raped by barbarians. She is then reincarnated three times, followed by the witches, and wronged again by reincarnations of the barbarian leader until the modern age, when she comes back as his elderly mother-in-law and manages to defeat him. The Three then assure the barbarian that he would be reincarnated as each of the priestesses he had raped, in order, with the exception of Ursula. He would never know what was happening until the moment of death, at which point it would start all over again. The Three are satisfied, and in the end decide that Ursula will live another twenty years and become an accomplished and respected witch in her twilight years, and her grandchild will be beautiful.

In the podcast, the Mother is voiced by [Ellen Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Thomas_/(actress/) "Ellen Thomas (actress)"), the Crone is voiced by [Cathy Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathy_Tyson "Cathy Tyson"), and the Maiden is voiced by [Sandra Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandra_Dickinson "Sandra Dickinson").

In the Netflix series, the Mother is portrayed by [Nina Wadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Wadia "Nina Wadia"), the Crone is portrayed by [Souad Faress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souad_Faress "Souad Faress"), and the Maiden is portrayed by [Dinita Gohil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinita_Gohil "Dinita Gohil").

**[Calliope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calliope "Calliope")** is one of the [Muses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muses "Muses"). She has had a history with Dream's Morpheus alias where they fathered [Orpheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheus "Orpheus").

In 1927, Calliope became a prisoner of Erasmus Fry after he found her bathing in a stream on Mount Helicon. He raped her for inspiration. By 1986, Fry gave Calliope to struggling author Richard Madoc and he used her inspiration to write his stories. By the time Dream was freed from his imprisonment, he helped to free her by flooding Richard's mind with too many inspirations. When Richard declared Calliope free, Calliope left to ensure that none of her fellow Muses would get trapped like she did.

In the podcast, Calliope is voiced by Samantha Béart.

In the Netflix series, Calliope is portrayed by [Melissanthi Mahut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissanthi_Mahut "Melissanthi Mahut").

The goddess **[Ishtar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishtar "Ishtar")**, disguised as an exotic dancer; a former lover of [Destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_/(DC_Comics/) "Destruction (DC Comics)").

In the Netflix series, Ishtar is portrayed by [Amber Rose Revah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber_Rose_Revah "Amber Rose Revah").

**Pharamond** is a former god, last of his pantheon, and a friend of Dream. At Dream's suggestion that he change with the times or fade like many other gods, Pharamond now runs a [travel agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_agency "Travel agency") in Dublin, under the [alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym") 'Mr Farrell'. He helps Dream and Delirium find the missing Destruction, and later provides assistance to Lucifer in his own series.

In the podcast, Pharamond is voiced by [Colin McFarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_McFarlane "Colin McFarlane").

The Norse God **[Thor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thor_in_comics#DC_Comics "Thor in comics")** first appeared in DC Comics in _Tales of the Unexpected_ #16 (August 1957), "The Magic Hammer", illustrated by [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby").

In another story attributed to Kirby and [George Papp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Papp "George Papp"), "The Magic Stick" in _House of Mystery_ #68 (November 1957), he looked like a traditional Viking with red hair, and his hammer looked identical to the way Kirby would draw it for [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thor_/(Marvel_Comics/) "Thor (Marvel Comics)"). That story was reprinted in _DC Special_ #4 (July 1969), which also contains Abel's debut.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-21) Kirby also pitted Wesley Dodds against someone claiming to be Thor in _[Adventure Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_Comics "Adventure Comics")_ #75 (June 1942).

Later, a museum worker named Henry Meke handled Thor's hammer and briefly became Thor during thunderstorms in _Batman_ #127 (October 1959).

In _Season of Mist_, Thor accompanied Odin and Loki to the Dreaming in order to get the Key to Hell from him. At one point, Thor had difficulty with the gate keepers upon his arrival.

In _The Kindly Ones_, Odin and Thor take Loki back to his punishment for kidnapping Daniel Hall and causing the Three to kill Dream.

Thor also appears in _[War of the Gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Gods_/(comics/) "War of the Gods (comics)")_ and _[Jack Kirby's Fourth World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby%27s_Fourth_World "Jack Kirby's Fourth World")_ (The Thor seen in _The Sandman_ does not resemble the one seen in the other DC comics).

In the podcast, Thor is voiced by Mitch Benn.

In the Netflix series, Thor is portrayed by [Laurence O'Fuarain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_O%27Fuarain "Laurence O'Fuarain"). Unlike the comics, he and Odin show up before the second Corinthian can eat Loki's eyes and take Loki back to his imprisonment.

**[Anubis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anubis "Anubis")** is the Egyptian God of the Underworld who is among the angels, deities, and demons that meet in the Dreaming to discuss the future of Hell following Lucifer's abdication. In the podcast, Anubis is voiced by Doug Devaney.

**[Bes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bes "Bes")** is an Egyptian [house deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_deity "House deity") who is among the angels, deities, and demons that meet in the Dreaming to discuss the future of Hell following Lucifer's abdication.

**[Susano-o-no-Mikoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susanoo-no-Mikoto "Susanoo-no-Mikoto")** is the [Japanese god](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kami "Kami") of the Sea, Storms, and Fields who is among the angels, deities, and demons that meet in the Dreaming to discuss the future of Hell following Lucifer's abdications.

In the podcast, Susano-o-no-Mikoto is voiced by Dai Tabuchi.

In the Netflix series, Susano-o-no-Mikoto is portrayed by Kristofer Kamiyasu.

**Kilderkin** is a member of the [Lords of Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_of_Order "Lords of Order") who was dispatched by his fellow Lords of Order to attend a meeting in the Dreaming with the other angels, deities, and demons to discuss the future of Hell following Lucifer's abdication.

In the Netflix series, Kilderkin sent an unnamed servant (portrayed by Andre Flynn) to represent him at the gathering in the Dreaming and forward the written messages in the servant's cubic box to Dream.

**Shivering Jemmy** is a child-like member of the [Lords of Chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_of_Chaos_and_Order "Lords of Chaos and Order") who was dispatched by her fellow Lords of Chaos to attend a meeting in the Dreaming with the other angels, deities, and demons to discuss the future of Hell following Lucifer's abdication.

In the podcast, Shivering Jemmy is voiced by [Lizzie Waterworth-Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizzie_Waterworth-Santo "Lizzie Waterworth-Santo").

In the Netflix series, Shivering Jemmy is portrayed by Lyla Quinn as a young girl and by Sue Muand as an elderly woman.

**[Hades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades_/(DC_Comics/) "Hades (DC Comics)")** is the God of the Greek underworld. His history with Orpheus remains intact.

In the podcast, Hades is voiced by [Toby Longworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Longworth "Toby Longworth").

In the Netflix series, Hades is portrayed by [Garry Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Cooper "Garry Cooper").

**[Persephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persephone "Persephone")** is the Queen of the Greek underworld. Her history with Orpheus remains intact.

In the Netflix series, Persephone is portrayed by Antonia Desplat.

Angels, fallen angels, and demons
---------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=63 "Edit section: Angels, fallen angels, and demons")\]

The following characters are either [angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel "Angel"), [fallen angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallen_angel "Fallen angel"), or [demons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demon "Demon"):

**Azazel** is a demon and a former ruler of Hell, reigning for a time alongside [Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)") and [Beelzebub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Beelzebub). Based on a statement from Agony and Ecstasy in _[Hellblazer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellblazer "Hellblazer")_ #12, he may have usurped his position from [Belial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belial "Belial") (described at the time was the third member of the triumvirate). He appears as a ragged opening into darkness, full of disembodied eyes and mouths. He was cast out after Lucifer abandoned Hell and later imprisoned by Dream in a glass jar. He reappears, still in Dream's glass jar, in _[Lucifer Volume 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/)#Volume_2_\(2015%E2%80%932017\) "Lucifer (DC Comics)")_ (2015).

He is based on the demon [Azazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azazel "Azazel").

Azazel first appeared in DC Comics battling [Madame Xanadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madame_Xanadu "Madame Xanadu") in the story intended for _Doorway to Nightmare_ #6 (it was cancelled after #5) that was eventually published in _[Cancelled Comic Cavalcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancelled_Comic_Cavalcade "Cancelled Comic Cavalcade")_ #2 and _[The Unexpected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unexpected_/(1968_comic_book/) "The Unexpected (1968 comic book)")_ #190. As with Lucifer's appearance in _The Brave and the Bold_, he looked more like a traditional devil, but was identified as an [incubus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incubus "Incubus"): here, a creature who steals people's dreams and imprints them upon tapestries that give him power, and cannot be destroyed without killing the victims.

In the podcast, Azazel is voiced by [Kerry Shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Shale "Kerry Shale").

In the Netflix series, Azazel is voiced by [Roger Allam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Allam "Roger Allam") in his ragged opening into darkness form during season one and by Wil Coban in his humanoid form during season two while also voicing his ragged opening into darkness form.

Along with Lucifer and Azazel, **Beelzebub** is a demon who was the third King of Hell. He often appears as either a gigantic green [fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly "Fly") or a fly's head on two short human legs. Sometimes, a human face can be seen between the fly's eyes. His constant buzzing slurs his speech (for example, 'Bbbbut nooo. Itzzz a Triummmvirate.').

He is based on the demon [Beelzebub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beelzebub "Beelzebub").

In the podcast, Beezlebug is voiced by [Ray Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Porter "Ray Porter").

**Choronzon** is a demon and a former duke of Hell who served under [Beelzebub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Beelzebub). He has pink skin and two mouths, one under the other.

Chronozon had possession of Dream's helm, but lost it in a challenge where he had Lucifer fight Dream on his behalf. He later reappeared briefly as one of [Azazel's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Azazel) tactics to gain ownership of Hell.

Choronzon is based on the demon [Choronzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choronzon "Choronzon").

Choronzon appears in _[52](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52_/(comics/) "52 (comics)")_ #25 (Late October 2006).

In the podcast, Chorozon is voiced by [Paterson Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paterson_Joseph "Paterson Joseph").

In the Netflix series, Choronzon is portrayed by [Munya Chawawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munya_Chawawa "Munya Chawawa").

**Duma** is a fallen angel from the [DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics") [Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_Comics "Vertigo Comics") series _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(comic_book/) "The Sandman (comic book)")_. Duma's name means "silence", and he is based on the angel [Duma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumah_/(angel/) "Dumah (angel)") from [Jewish mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_mythology "Jewish mythology").

In _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Season_of_Mists "The Sandman: Season of Mists")_, [Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_comics/) "Lucifer (DC comics)") abdicates Hell and gives the key to Dream until God assigns Duma and [Remiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Remiel) to take control of Hell.

Remiel and Duma lose ownership of Hell in the _Lucifer_ spin-off series. Duma eventually allies with Lucifer and Elaine Belloc to save creation and persuades Hell's new ruler Christopher Rudd to bring his army to Heaven's aid at the Battle of [Armageddon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armageddon "Armageddon").

In the Netflix series, Duma is portrayed by Rilwan Abiola Owokoniran.

**Lucifer** is the sometime ruler of Hell and a fallen angel. He is based on the fallen angel [Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer "Lucifer"), whose story was created by [John Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in his epic poem _[Paradise Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise_Lost "Paradise Lost")_.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-22) Neil Gaiman also used the character Lucifer in his short story 'Murder Mysteries', wherein he was a captain in the Silver City, with [Azazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azazel "Azazel") as his protégé.

In the book "Hanging out with the Dream King" (a book consisting of interviews with Gaiman's collaborators), one of Gaiman's artists, Kelley Jones, states that Lucifer's appearance is based on that of [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"):

> Neil was adamant that the Devil was David Bowie. He just said, "He is. You _must_ draw David Bowie. Find David Bowie, or I'll send you David Bowie. Because if it isn't David Bowie, you're going to have to redo it until it _is_ David Bowie." So I said, "Okay, it's David Bowie."

Lucifer made at least three previous appearances in DC Comics (_[Superman's Pal Jimmy Olsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman%27s_Pal_Jimmy_Olsen "Superman's Pal Jimmy Olsen")_ #65, _[Weird Mystery Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_Mystery_Tales "Weird Mystery Tales")_ #4, and _DC Special Series_ #8, a.k.a. _[The Brave and the Bold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brave_and_the_Bold "The Brave and the Bold") Special_), but his appearance was more traditional. Lucifer as he appeared in _The Sandman_ also appeared in issues of the series _[The Demon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etrigan_the_Demon "Etrigan the Demon")_ (vol. 3) and _[The Spectre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectre_/(DC_Comics_character/) "Spectre (DC Comics character)")_ (vol. 2) and in the miniseries _[Stanley and His Monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_and_His_Monster "Stanley and His Monster")_ (vol. 2).

In the podcast, Lucifer is voiced by [Michael Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sheen "Michael Sheen").

In the Netflix series, Lucifer is genderbent (but still physically accurate to her comic variant) and portrayed by [Gwendoline Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwendoline_Christie "Gwendoline Christie").

**Mazikeen** is a fictional character from [Neil Gaiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gaiman "Neil Gaiman")'s _[Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(comic_book/) "The Sandman (comic book)")_ [mythos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythology "Mythology"). The name "[Mazikeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazikeen "Mazikeen")" comes from that of a shapeshifting demon of [Jewish mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_mythology "Jewish mythology").

Mazikeen first appeared in _The Sandman_, where she was [Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)")'s consort while he reigned in Hell. At the time, half of her face was normal, but the other half was horribly misshapen and skeletal, causing her speech to be nearly unintelligible. (Gaiman wrote Mazikeen's dialogue by trying to speak using only half of his mouth, and writing down phonetically what came out.)

When Lucifer resigned, Mazikeen left Hell and ended up following her master, becoming part of the staff at the "Lux" (Latin for _light_, and the first root word in "Lucifer"), an elite Los Angeles bar that Lucifer had opened and played piano at. To conceal her demonic nature, she covered the deformed half of her face with a white mask and rarely spoke.

In the ongoing comic book series _[Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)")_, Mazikeen is a devoted ally of Lucifer Morningstar and the war leader of the [Lilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilin "Lilin"), a race descended from [Lilith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilith "Lilith"). A fearsome warrior and a respected leader, Mazikeen is a prominent character in the Lucifer comics. She has the appearance of a human female with long black hair.

In _Lucifer_, Mazikeen's face was turned fully human when she was resuscitated by the [Basanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Basanos) following the destruction of the Lux in a fire. This was because the vessel of the Basanos, Jill Presto, did not realize that Mazikeen's face was naturally deformed, and assumed that it was burned in the fire.

When Lucifer refused to assist her in restoring her face to its former state, she defected to her family, the Lilim-in-Exile. As their war leader, she led their army against Lucifer's cosmos, allying herself briefly with the Basanos. However, this was a ruse; after a desperate gamble, she bought Lucifer enough time to destroy the Basanos and regain control of his creation. Lucifer then accepted her into his service once more and made the Lilim-in-Exile the standing army of his universe.

Lucifer ultimately restores Mazikeen's half-skeletal face shortly before departing the known universes.

In the podcast, Mazikeen is voiced by Karen Batke.

In the Netflix series, Mazikeen is portrayed by Lesley-Ann Brandt. She has a few lines of dialogue and serves as Lucifer's servant and bodyguard.

**Remiel** is an [angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel "Angel") in the comic book series _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(comics/) "The Sandman (comics)")_; based on the angel [Remiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remiel "Remiel"). He first appears in _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Season_of_Mists "The Sandman: Season of Mists")_. In Biblical and Judaic traditions, Remiel is an [Archangel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archangel "Archangel") and a _[Grigori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watcher_/(angel/) "Watcher (angel)")_; a [Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choir "Choir")/[Hierarchy of angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchy_of_angels "Hierarchy of angels"), whose role is to observe humanity, lending a helping hand when necessary but not interfere.

Remiel, along with [Duma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Duma), is sent to observe when [Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_/(character/) "Dream (character)") is given the key to [Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell "Hell"). Dream finally gives the key to Remiel and Duma, and the two angels descend to Hell to rule over the countless sinners and demons there.

Following the end of the _Sandman_ series, Remiel and Duma lose ownership of Hell in the _[Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)")_ spin-off series. At the end of the series, Remiel tries to rebel against [Elaine Belloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Belloc "Elaine Belloc"), refusing to accept her as God's successor. When he tries to kill Gaudium and Spera, friends of Elaine's, she puts him in his own Hell until he reforms.

In the podcast, Remiel is voiced by [Adrian Lester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Lester "Adrian Lester").

In the Netflix series, Remiel is portrayed by Jake Fairbrother.

### Minor angels and demons

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=71 "Edit section: Minor angels and demons")\]

**Squatterbloat** is a rhyme-speaking demon who serves as the Gatekeeper of Hell.

In the Netflix series, Squatterbloat is performed by Martyn Ford.

**Ketele** is a demon in Hell who doubted that Lucifer was originally from Heaven during Dream's second visit to Hell and prior to Lucifer's abdication.

**Rimmon-My-Petal** is a demon in Hell who doubted that Lucifer was originally from Heaven during Dream's second visit to Hell and prior to Lucifer's abdication.

#### Merkin, Mother of Spiders

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=75 "Edit section: Merkin, Mother of Spiders")\]

First appeared in _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season_of_Mists "Season of Mists")_, **Merkin, Mother of Spiders** is an envoy with Azazel. A lumpen, hideous, vaguely feminine figure, whose womb produces [spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider "Spider"). The Merkin's facial form was almost certainly based upon a photograph by the artist [Joel-Peter Witkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel-Peter_Witkin "Joel-Peter Witkin") entitled "Amour, New Mexico, 1987", showing a naked female figure wearing a spider-like horned mask.

In the podcast, Merkin is voiced by [Clare Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_Corbett "Clare Corbett").

In the Netflix series, Merikin is portrayed by Olamide Candide-Johnson. This version is shown to have retractable spider legs coming out of her torso.

The following are inhabitants of [Faerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faerie_/(DC_Comics/) "Faerie (DC Comics)"):

The **Cluracan** is a [courtier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtier "Courtier") of the Queen of Faerie and the brother to [Nuala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Nuala), the Dream King's fairy servant. An amoral, merry, capricious, pansexual rogue, Cluracan features in _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Season_of_Mists "The Sandman: Season of Mists")_, _[Worlds' End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Worlds%27_End "The Sandman: Worlds' End")_, _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_, and _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_. He is strongly reminiscent of the "[trickster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trickster "Trickster")" archetype also associated with [Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Loki).

Following the events of _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_, Cluracan offends his queen so badly that she sends him to the court of Llinor, where tradition demands that he marry a lady of the royal house; whereupon Cluracan's [nemesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archenemy "Archenemy") – identical to him in every way except his sexual orientation – takes Cluracan's place.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-23)

The Cluracan is named after a drunken [leprechaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leprechaun "Leprechaun") of [Irish mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_mythology "Irish mythology"), the [Cluricaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluricaun "Cluricaun").

In the podcast, Cluracan is voiced by [Aidan Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aidan_Turner "Aidan Turner").

In the Netflix series, Cluracan is portrayed by [Douglas Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Booth "Douglas Booth").

**Nuala** is a [faerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy "Fairy") given to Dream at the end of _[Season of Mists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Season_of_Mists "The Sandman: Season of Mists")_ who takes on the [housekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housekeeping "Housekeeping") duties of the Dreaming.

Nuala stops her duties when her brother [Cluracan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Cluracan) takes her back to Faerie in _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_. When she leaves, Dream grants her permission to summon him at need. When she asks to become his paramour, he refuses.

She subsequently appears in the _Sandman_ spinoff series _[The Dreaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dreaming_/(comics/) "The Dreaming (comics)")_.

In the podcast, Nuala is voiced by [Niamh Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niamh_Walsh "Niamh Walsh").

In the Netflix series, Nuala is portrayed by [Ann Skelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Skelly "Ann Skelly").

**Auberon** is a character in the comic book series _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(comic_book/) "The Sandman (comic book)")_ and _[The Books of Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Magic "The Books of Magic")_. He is seen for the first time in [_Sandman_ #19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Dream_Country#A_Midsummer_Night's_Dream "The Sandman: Dream Country") as Auberon of Dom-Daniel where he and Titania accompanied Dream in seeing the production of _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Midsummer_Night%27s_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_.

Auberon appears again in several issues of _[The Books of Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Magic "The Books of Magic")_ and in the _[Books of Faerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Faerie "The Books of Faerie")_ miniseries.

The character was inspired by [Oberon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberon "Oberon") of [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s _A Midsummer Night's Dream_.

In the podcast, Auberon is voiced by [Toby Longworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Longworth "Toby Longworth").

In the Netflix series, Auberon is portrayed by [Royce Pierreson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royce_Pierreson "Royce Pierreson").

**Titania** is the queen of the [fay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy "Fairy"); she first appears in [issue #19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Dream_Country#A_Midsummer_Night's_Dream "The Sandman: Dream Country"). The character was inspired by [Shakespeare's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") [Titania (Fairy Queen)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titania_/(Fairy_Queen/) "Titania (Fairy Queen)") in the play _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Midsummer_Night%27s_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_. There is implication that she in the past was a lover of Dream's, although this is never confirmed. Auberon and Titania accompanied Dream in seeing the production of _A Midsummer Night's Dream_ where Titania was accompanied by her court of boggarts, elves, fairies, goblins, nixies, and trolls.

Titania is also a major character in the comic book _[The Books of Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Magic "The Books of Magic")_, of which the first four issues were written by Gaiman, and its spin-off series _[The Books of Faerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Faerie "The Books of Faerie")_. In the latter series, it is revealed that she was a human girl who crossed over into the fay realm and was then adopted by the previous queen of the fay, and received her faerie powers from a circlet seized by her from that queen. Despite this power, it was revealed that she is [illiterate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy"), and so regularly uses Dream's library because its special properties allow its users to read books in any language, including those they cannot speak. There are suggestions that she may be the mother of the series' protagonist, [Timothy Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Hunter_/(DC_Comics/) "Tim Hunter (DC Comics)").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-No51-24)

In the podcast, Titania is voiced by Felicity Duncan.

In the Netflix series, Titania is portrayed by [Ruta Gedmintas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruta_Gedmintas "Ruta Gedmintas").

**Puck** is a brown-furred [trickster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trickster "Trickster") and [hobgoblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobgoblin "Hobgoblin"), who appears several times in _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(comic_book/) "The Sandman (comic book)")_.

He is seen for the first time in [_Sandman_ #19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Dream_Country#A_Midsummer_Night's_Dream "The Sandman: Dream Country") where he was among those who accompanied Auberon and Titania where they joined Dream in seeing the production of _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Midsummer_Night%27s_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_.

In _The Kindly Ones_, Puck aids the Norse God Loki in kidnapping [Daniel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Hall_/(comics/) "Daniel Hall (comics)"), playing a small role in the death of Dream and Daniel's subsequent assuming of the title by assisting Loki in capturing Daniel.

Puck later appeared in an issue of _[The Books of Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Books_of_Magic "The Books of Magic")_, hiding as a gangster called Mr. Robbins in [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") whose true nature is discovered—but not exposed—by [Timothy Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Hunter_/(DC_Comics/) "Tim Hunter (DC Comics)").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-No63-25) The character was inspired by [Puck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puck_/(Shakespeare/) "Puck (Shakespeare)") of [Shakespeare's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Midsummer_Night%27s_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_.

In the podcast, Puck is voiced by [Kerry Shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Shale "Kerry Shale").

In the Netflix series, Puck is portrayed by [Jack Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gleeson "Jack Gleeson").

Immortals, witches, and long-lived humans
-----------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=82 "Edit section: Immortals, witches, and long-lived humans")\]

The following characters are either immortals, witches, or long-lived humans:

**Robert "Hob" Gadling** is a human granted immortality, who meets with [Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_/(character/) "Dream (character)") once every hundred years.

Hob was granted immortality in a pub named the White Horse in 1389 when he simply declared that he "had decided never to die"; whereupon Death agrees, at Dream's request, to forgo him. Hob thereupon takes to a variety of occupations over the centuries, including slaving, and periodically reinvents himself as a descendant of his previous persona. Gradually, he acquires a conscience and by the 20th century, he has become full of remorse at his past deeds. Dream converses with Gadling once per century, of Gadling's latest occupations. At their 20th century meeting, Dream admits that the purpose of the exercise was simply for him to have a friend.

In _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_, Death offers to end his six-hundred-year life. Gadling declines.

In the podcast, Hob Gadling is voiced by [Matthew Horne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Horne "Matthew Horne").

In the Netflix series, Hob is portrayed by [Ferdinand Kingsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Kingsley "Ferdinand Kingsley").

**Orpheus** is the son of Dream and the muse [Calliope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Calliope). He is based on [Orpheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheus "Orpheus") of [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology").

In "[The Song of Orpheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Fables_and_Reflections#%22The_Song_of_Orpheus%22 "The Sandman: Fables and Reflections")", the Endless attend Orpheus's wedding to Eurydice. Eurydice dies on the same night and Orpheus asks his father to retrieve her from the [Greek underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_underworld "Greek underworld"). Dream refuses, but Orpheus gets help from Destruction and Death. As in the legend, Orpheus travels to Hades, plays his sad music to Hades and Persephone, loses Eurydice again when he looks at her spirit during departure, and gets torn apart by the [Bacchanae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maenad "Maenad") (the beloved madwomen of [Dionysus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysus "Dionysus")). Because of his immortality, Orpheus survives as a disembodied head. Dream establishes a priesthood to take care of his son, saying that they will never meet again.

In "[Thermidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Fables_and_Reflections#%22Thermidor%22 "The Sandman: Fables and Reflections")", Johanna Constantine is asked by Dream to rescue Orpheus from [Revolutionary France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_France "Revolutionary France"). Orpheus's singing stuns [Maximilien Robespierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Robespierre "Maximilien Robespierre") and [Louis de Saint-Just](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_de_Saint-Just "Louis de Saint-Just"), leading to the [Thermidorian Reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermidorian_Reaction "Thermidorian Reaction"). Orpheus misses his father who still has not visited him.

In _[Brief Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Brief_Lives "The Sandman: Brief Lives")_, Dream has to talk to Orpheus in order to find Destruction. In return, Orpheus is granted his wish of death enabling him to pass on and reunite with Eurydice in the afterlife. This would later come back to bite Orpheus in _[The Sandman: The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_ when the Three's Erinyes aspect mentions him spilling family blood.

In the podcast, Orpheus is voiced by [Regé-Jean Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reg%C3%A9-Jean_Page "Regé-Jean Page").

In the Netflix series, Orpheus is portrayed by [Ruairi O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruairi_O%27Connor "Ruairi O'Connor"). Unlike the comics, Destruction and Death help Orpheus get into the Greek underworld.

**Thessaly** is the last of the millennia-old witches of Thessaly. She makes her first appearance in _[A Game of You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_A_Game_of_You "The Sandman: A Game of You")_. She has a bookish appearance with straight hair and thick glasses that belie her personality: amoral, cold-blooded, proud, and ruthless, though not malicious. She will kill people who are potential threats with no hesitation or remorse.

[Neil Gaiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gaiman "Neil Gaiman") named this character after the land of witches, [Thessaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaly "Thessaly"), in [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"). In one of Plato's dialogues, the Gorgias, Socrates states "I would not have us risk that which is dearest on the acquisition of this power, like the Thessalian enchantresses, who, as they say, bring down the moon from heaven at the risk of their own perdition." In the series, Thessaly does exactly that, with deadly consequences, just as Socrates predicts. Later in the series, Thessaly changes her name to [Larissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larissa "Larissa"), which is the capital of Thessaly. Larissa was actually the local fountain nymph, after whom the town was named. It is suggested however that Thessaly is even older than this civilization and may date from Neolithic times. In a later series,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-26) Thessaly tells someone her name is [Lamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamia "Lamia"). "Lamia" refers to several types of monster, and to other magical and supernatural characters, in [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), as well as to the Thessalian witches Meroe and Panthia in _[The Golden Ass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Ass "The Golden Ass")_ by [Apuleius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apuleius "Apuleius").

Thessaly returns in the later volumes, where she is Dream's lover for a time, but this relationship ends unhappily for both and is never actually shown in the series. When it is alluded to in _[Brief Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Brief_Lives "The Sandman: Brief Lives")_ Thessaly is never mentioned by name, so only in _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_ is this romance revealed. Also in _The Kindly Ones_, Thessaly provides [Lyta Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fury_/(DC_Comics/) "Fury (DC Comics)") with protection and sanctuary from Dream while he is being targeted for death by the Furies, who are using Hall as a vessel.

In _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_ she attends Dream's wake and funeral. Thessaly speaks with two of Dream's lovers and recalls her relationship with Dream. She remarks that part of his attraction to her was that she was not intimidated by him. To her surprise she later would dream of Morpheus, and the two kindled a romance, with Dream madly in love with Thessaly (though this affection was not mutual). When Morpheus ended his courtship and resumed working Thessaly realized she did not love Morpheus and left the Dreaming. When Lyta wakes up after Dream's death, Thessaly calmly advises her to leave. Thessaly suggests that many people, including herself, would be more than happy to murder Lyta for her part in Morpheus' destruction.

Thessaly also is the star of two spin-off comic series, _The Thessaliad_ and _Thessaly, Witch for Hire_ written by [Bill Willingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Willingham "Bill Willingham"). In the spin-offs, Thessaly (under that name) and her companion, a ghost named Fetch, first set out to tackle various gods of the underworld who want her dead. Later she is unwillingly pressured into a monster-killing contract.

She is alluded to in the _[Faction Paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faction_Paradox "Faction Paradox")_ series, in the character Thessalia and her protégé Larissa.

In the podcast, Thessaly is voiced by [Emma Corrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Corrin "Emma Corrin").

**Mad Hettie** is a London tramp born in 1741. At the time of _Sandman_ #3, she was 247 years old. Mad Hettie appears frequently in other DC comics such as _Hellblazer_, first appearing in #9. She also had a large role in _Death: The High Cost of Living_, where she is shown to be rude, miserly and constantly complains about the lack of knowledge that present day youths have. She has been accused of being a witch and also appears to have abilities as a [haruspex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haruspex "Haruspex"). However, she merely states that "you don't get to your two hundred and fiftieth without learning a few tricks".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-vert-deat-27)

Later, Hettie worked in the series _The Dreaming_ in which it was discovered that she had dealings with [Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny_/(DC_Comics_character/) "Destiny (DC Comics character)"), [Johanna Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Johanna_Constantine) and President [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson").

In _The Sandman: Overture_, it is revealed that she had stolen a magical timepiece in her youth, which remained hidden in her memories until Daniel retrieved it.

In the podcast, Mad Hettie is voiced by [Josie Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josie_Lawrence "Josie Lawrence").

In the Netflix series, Mad Hettie is portrayed by [Clare Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_Higgins "Clare Higgins").

Appearing for the first time in _Lucifer: Nirvana_, the **Silk Man** is an immortal sorcerer, described by [Lucifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucifer_/(DC_Comics/) "Lucifer (DC Comics)") as "a fossil remnant from an earlier, cruder creation. His body is a weaving that has to be renewed constantly. Silk Man's spirit too, come to that. A messy form of immortality, but it seems to do the job." In earlier days, Silk Man was the leader of the Arao Jinn. He appears as a mercenary, hired by the angel Perdissa to kill Lucifer. Silk Man seems to need to consume living things to stay alive, weaving them into himself. He is severely damaged by Perdissa and eventually killed by Lucifer.

In "[The Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_Fables_and_Reflections "The Sandman: Fables and Reflections")", **Vassily** appears as an old man telling his teen-aged granddaughter a tale from "the old country", Russia. A youth raised in a remote forest has a series of adventures, including meeting with Lucien (to whom he gives a book) and [Baba Yaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baba_Yaga "Baba Yaga"), and marrying a fellow shape-changing wolf. At the end of the story, it is revealed that the grandfather is the youth in his own story.

The following are known mortals:

**Roderick Burgess** (1863–1947), born **Morris Burgess Brocklesby** and known also as **The Daemon King**, was the Lord Magus of The Order of the Ancient Mysteries. His magical fraternity was based in "Fawney Rig" in [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex "Sussex"), and was initially funded by his inherited industrial wealth. Burgess is a magician rather in the vein of the real [Aleister Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleister_Crowley "Aleister Crowley"), and within the [DC world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Universe "DC Universe") is Crowley's rival.

The series begins with Burgess' attempt to capture and bind [Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_/(DC_Comics/) "Death (DC Comics)"), which fails, capturing [Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_/(character/) "Dream (character)") instead. Burgess keeps Dream trapped in a glass globe for the rest of his (Burgess') life, attempting to bargain with Dream, but Dream remains silent. Burgess dies from a heart attack still attempting to get a response out of Dream. His order passes the globe and Dream to his son Alex.

Burgess is a bald-headed, slightly pot-bellied man with a large hook nose. He is ultimately self-centred; his sole purpose for the Order is to bring money and power to himself, and he is consumed by his desire to achieve immortality. His relationship with his son is only briefly touched on, though it is implied that it is unhealthy, with Burgess pushing his son to spend his life pursuing his father's dreams.

In the podcast, Roderick Burgess is voiced by [Stephen Critchlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Critchlow "Stephen Critchlow").

[Charles Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dance "Charles Dance") portrays the character in the television series _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(TV_series/) "The Sandman (TV series)")_ on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-28) This version of the character dies of a brain hemorrhage instead of a heart attack.

**Alex Burgess** is the son of Roderick Burgess, mother unknown (but probably [Ethel Cripps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Ethel_Cripps),\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] and therefore half-brother of [Doctor Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Destiny "Doctor Destiny")). He is taught by his father, and takes part in his rituals. Upon Roderick Burgess' death, Alex inherits his estate, including his magical order. He keeps Dream imprisoned, as his father did, trying to bargain for power and immortality in exchange for Dream's release.

The Order of the Ancient Mysteries enjoys a resurgence in popularity in the 1960s, but by the 1970s it is in decline again. Alex passes ownership of the Order on to his boyfriend, Paul McGuire, and becomes obsessed with his prisoner and with his father. Finally, in 1988, Dream escapes and puts Alex into a nightmare of "eternal waking", in which he is forever dreaming he is waking up, and each waking degenerates into another horrible nightmare. This nightmare lasts for years, ending only with Dream's death in _[The Kindly Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Kindly_Ones "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones")_.

Alex is quite tall and near-sighted. He has brown hair which he wears in a variety of styles throughout his life, but by old age he is bald and has come to resemble his father very closely. His relationship with McGuire is deep and heartfelt, but his obsessions with his father and with Dream eventually come to rule his life. In _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_, he appears again as the child that we see in his first appearance.

Alex is in many ways a tragic figure, perhaps the first statement of the theme that [Desire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desire_/(DC_Comics/) "Desire (DC Comics)") explores in _[The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_: "The bonds of family bind both ways". Had Alex not been born the son of his father, inheriting the imprisoned Dream, his life might have been much happier. However, he is finally able to find some measure of fulfillment in his old age, following Dream's death and also attends his funeral.

His name almost certainly derives from [Anthony Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Burgess "Anthony Burgess")'s _[A Clockwork Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Clockwork_Orange_/(novel/) "A Clockwork Orange (novel)")_, the protagonist of which is named Alex, but could also be a nod to [Aleister Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleister_Crowley "Aleister Crowley"), whose original middle name was Alexander and who was mentioned in the first issue.

In the podcast, Alex Burgess is voiced by [Blake Ritson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_Ritson "Blake Ritson").

Alex appears in _[The Sandman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman_/(TV_series/) "The Sandman (TV series)")_ episode "Sleep of the Just", portrayed by [Benjamin Evan Ainsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Evan_Ainsworth "Benjamin Evan Ainsworth") as a young man, [Laurie Kynaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurie_Kynaston "Laurie Kynaston") as an adult, Benedick Blythe as an elderly man in season one, and by [Geoffrey Beevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Beevers "Geoffrey Beevers") as an elderly man in season two. Unlike the comics, Dream later releases Alex from his "eternal waking" prior to creating the second Corinthian. Upon waking up, Alex calls for Paul, who runs in to Alex's bedroom to see Alex awake as they embrace each other.

**Ruthven Sykes** is a bespectacled Afro-Caribbean man with short hair.

He is [Roderick Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Roderick_Burgess)' second-in-command of the Order of the Ancient Mysteries until November 1930, when he steals a number of treasures (including Dream's helmet, ruby and pouch of sand) and £200,000 in cash from the order and flees to San Francisco with Roderick's mistress, [Ethel Cripps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Ethel_Cripps). In December 1930, he trades the helmet to the demon [Choronzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Choronzon) for an amulet that looks like an eyeball on a chain. This amulet protects him from the magics of Burgess until 1936 when Ethel Cripps leaves him taking the amulet with her. He is then killed.

In the podcast, Ruthven Sykes is voiced by [Oris Erhuero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oris_Erhuero "Oris Erhuero").

In the Netflix series, Ruthven Sykes is portrayed by [Ansu Kabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansu_Kabia "Ansu Kabia").

**Ethel Cripps**, also known as **Ethel Dee**, is the mother of [John Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Destiny "Doctor Destiny"). She was the mistress of [Roderick Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Roderick_Burgess) until she fled with [Ruthven Sykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Ruthven_Sykes).

Her last joy was her son, John Dee, whom she sought for 10 years. She discovered that he had become a living corpse, which happened because of his use of the Sandman's Ruby.

At this time, she was 90 years old, and it was alluded that she had been kept alive by an amulet in the shape of an eye which granted its user protection, the amulet that [Ruthven Sykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Ruthven_Sykes) had been given by the demon [Choronzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Choronzon) in exchange for Dream's helmet. Sykes, who had been second in command in The Order of Ancient Mysteries, needed protection from [Roderick Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#Roderick_Burgess) who was seeking retribution for Sykes' treachery of the theft of the £200,000 and Dream's magical items, which were in possession of the Order at the time he fled with Ethel Cripps to San Francisco in 1930. "Magical War" was declared upon them, and Ruthven knew he would need a way to protect himself from the hexes Burgess sought to put upon him.

In 1936, Ethel walked out on Ruthven, taking with her the amulet of protection and Dream's Ruby. While in his possession, the amulet protected Sykes from Burgess' hexes, but without it, he died a messy and painful death, with his insides exploding out of him. The amulet continued to protect Ethel while Choronzon was still in possession of Dream's helmet.

After Dream escaped and sought to regain his items, he descended to Hell to find his helmet. He had to battle Choronzon to regain it. After his victory, the compact was withdrawn and the power of protection the amulet possessed ended which also ended the life of Ethel Dee.

In the podcast, Ethel Cripps is voiced by Karen Bartke.

In the Netflix series, Ethel Cripps is portrayed by [Joely Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joely_Richardson "Joely Richardson") as an older woman and by [Niamh Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niamh_Walsh "Niamh Walsh") as a younger woman. Unlike the comics, Ethel gave the Amulet of Protection to her son before dying.

**Wesley Dodds**, also known as **Sandman**, is the original costumed crimefighter who used the name. According to Gaiman, he was merely filling a hole in the universe in a similar way to a process of evolution, in which animals fill up a niche—for instance, what should fly. He is first seen in _The Sandman_ series in a two-panel cameo in issue #1, and another cameo in issue #26. Dream occasionally appeared in dream sequences in Dodds's own series, _[Sandman Mystery Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandman_Mystery_Theatre "Sandman Mystery Theatre")_. The two finally met for real in Gaiman's _[Sandman Midnight Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandman_Midnight_Theatre "Sandman Midnight Theatre")_. Dodds appeared out of costume during _[The Sandman: The Wake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sandman:_The_Wake "The Sandman: The Wake")_ (#72). The reason for his prophetic visions is explained as him being embodied with a small portion of Dream's essence. His reasoning for assuming his role as The Sandman is given as nightmares of Dream in his helmet that plague him _until_ he begins his career as a crimefighter, after which "Wesley Dodds sleeps the **sleep** of the **Just**."

In the podcast, Wesley Dodds is voiced by [Ray Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Porter "Ray Porter").

### Johanna Constantine

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_The_Sandman_characters&action=edit&section=95 "Edit section: Johanna Constantine")\]

**Lady Johanna Constantine** is an 18th-century supernatural adventuress. Dream encounters her several times, once to ask her to recover the head of his son, [Orpheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheus "Orpheus") – a mission she performed so successfully that part of its aftereffects was the ending of the French Revolution's Reign of Terror.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-29)

In the _Hellblazer Special: Lady Constantine_ graphic novel, an ancient evil refers to Johanna Constantine as 'the Constantine', the 'laughing magician', and the 'constant one', all titles that have been used (usually by other ancient evils) to describe [John Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Constantine "John Constantine"). The evil taunts her, saying "did you think to trick us with a new form?" There is the implication that throughout all times there have been recurring incarnations of Constantine who contain the spark of magic.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-30) In the story Johanna Constantine learns that "the [Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil "Devil") and the [Wandering Jew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wandering_Jew "Wandering Jew")" meet once every hundred years in a London pub; this meeting is actually between Dream and Hob Gadling, as she discovers when she interrupts the meeting.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-31) The story's conclusion shows Johanna Constantine inheriting a property she calls "Fawney Rig", after the con job wherein a gilded ring is sold as though it were solid gold, the implication being that she attained the property through trickery. This property was later owned by Roderick Burgess, the mage who captures Dream in the beginning of _The Sandman_.

In her middle age, Johanna Constantine is charged by persons unknown with the key to a box containing the sigil of America, allegedly created by Destiny.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sandman_characters#cite_note-32) This is stolen and hidden in the future by the wanderer, Mad Hettie. Hettie both blackmails ("I knows about you and the little Corsican") and bribes Johanna for her silence, promising her that she would live to age 99. This promise proves true, with Johanna dying at age 99 while getting out of her wheelchair when she hears the song of her old companion Orpheus.

Johanna is an ancestor of [John Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Constantine "John Constantine"), as revealed in the miniseries _The Sandman Presents: Love Street_.

She is also mentioned in the _[Doctor Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who "Doctor Who")_ novel _[The Man in the Velvet Mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_in_the_Velvet_Mask "The Man in the Velvet Mask")_, set in an alternate post-Revolutionary France.

In the podcast, Johanna Constantine is voiced by [Joanna Lumley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanna_Lumley "Joanna Lumley").
